evidence_note: Crassus and Caesar formed a political alliance in 60 BCE. Crassus provided financial backing for Caesar's political career, including guaranteeing his debts before his Spanish propraetorship (61 BCE). The relationship was a political partnership, not a personal friendship — sources do not portray closeness or mutual affection. Caesar left the crucial meeting at Luca (56 BCE) to renew the triumvirate.

Crassus and Pompey were political rivals throughout their parallel careers. They were joint consuls in 70 BCE (tension-filled) and again in 55 BCE (arranged at Luca). Plutarch records their mutual suspicion and competition for military glory and political influence. Their rivalry predated the triumvirate and continued within it.

Crassus and Cicero had a complex political relationship. Cicero defended Crassus in a legal case and sought his political support. Crassus was a potential ally of the optimates when it suited him, and Cicero navigated between him and Pompey. Cicero's letters (Att. 2.9, Fam. 1.9) mention Crassus as a political actor. They were fellow senators and at times allies, but not close friends.

Crassus's son Publius served with distinction under Caesar in Gaul (58-56 BCE), commanding cavalry at the Battle of the Sabis (57 BCE) and in Aquitania (56 BCE). He joined his father's Parthian expedition and was killed at Carrhae in 53 BCE. His death was a devastating blow to Crassus personally.

Crassus commanded the Roman forces that defeated the slave rebellion led by Spartacus (73-71 BCE). He decisively defeated Spartacus's main army in 71 BCE and crucified approximately 6,000 captured rebels. Spartacus himself was killed in the final battle, though his body was never identified.

Surena was the Parthian general (spahbed) who commanded the Parthian forces at Carrhae. He employed horse archers and cataphracts to devastating effect against Crassus's heavy infantry. According to Plutarch, Surena had Crassus killed after a parley went wrong. Surena himself was later executed by the Parthian king Orodes II, reportedly out of jealousy at his victory.
